requirement_text.REQ-159: First of two sibling requirements splitting R-Co's eight-function platform.* surface along the read/write seam. This one covers the functions that only READ or EMIT and stage nothing: platform.read_variable (LUA-11's read half), platform.get_instance_state, and platform.log (LUA-13). platform.now already shipped in REQ-152, not re-implemented here. LUA-11 read half: 'platform.read_variable(name) MUST return the current value or nil.' LUA-13 (Logging, MUST): 'platform.log(level, message, context) MUST emit a structured log entry tagged with the script's identity, instance ID, and trace ID,' acceptance 'Log entry appears with correct correlation IDs.' NUMBER MARSHALLING IS NOT THIS REQUIREMENT'S TO DECIDE -- REQ-150 settles OQ-6 centrally (lib/letflow/design/req150-lua-number-marshalling.md) and names Letflow.Engine.LuaNumberMarshalling (lib/letflow/engine/lua_number_marshalling.ex, does NOT exist yet -- REQ-159 creates it per REQ-150's naming) with to_lua/1 and from_lua/1, both identity functions for numeric/nil cases. This requirement cites REQ-150's normative section by number and uses that conversion; it must not introduce a second rule. CAPABILITY GATES, from R-Co's host_api matrix: read_variable requires variable:read; get_instance_state requires instance:read; log requires audit:log. Each is checked via REQ-157's Capabilities.check!/3 at its own call site -- LUA-06's 'at call site' is structural, not decorative. TENANT BOUNDARY, per decision 0014 (e): neither runtime is given database access. Host functions receive already-resolved values; the tenant prefix is supplied by the calling engine code and is NEVER derived inside a script or read from a script-supplied argument. A read_variable implementation that reaches Letflow.Repo directly with a prefix taken from script input is a tenant-isolation defect, not an optimization. NOT IN THIS REQUIREMENT: platform.write_variable, call_service, emit_event (REQ-160); platform.fail (REQ-161). GATE: SECURITY-REVIEWER is a hard gate. Queue task 311, GH#611. See docs/requirements.yaml REQ-159 for full description and acceptance_criteria.

task.description: CODE-DESIGNER (WF-02 Step 1) for REQ-159. Write lib/letflow/design/req159-lua-host-api-read.md. Read lib/letflow/engine/lua/platform.ex in full (REQ-157's current state -- the 6 gated functions are currently stubs that raise a labeled 'not yet implemented' error after the capability check passes; this requirement replaces 3 of those 6 stubs -- read_variable, get_instance_state, log -- with real implementations, without touching the other 3 (write_variable, call_service, emit_event, which are REQ-160's) or now/fail). Read lib/letflow/design/req150-lua-number-marshalling.md's Section 3 in full (names Letflow.Engine.LuaNumberMarshalling, to_lua/1, from_lua/1 -- this module does not exist yet and REQ-159 must create it, per that design's own instruction that REQ-159/160 create it, not each inventing separately). Read lib/letflow/design/req157-lua-capability-model.md for Capabilities.check!/3's exact signature. Read lib/letflow/instances.ex (Letflow.Instances.get_by_id/2 -- the established pattern for reading an InstanceProjection by id with an explicit prefix, never derived from caller input) and lib/letflow/event_store/instance_projection.ex (confirm the :variables jsonb field and :status field shapes). Also read the current platform.ex's install/2 fold mechanism (from REQ-157/155/156) to understand exactly how a matrix row's stub gets replaced with a real implementation without disturbing the fold's single-registration-point invariant. Also write test/specs/REQ-159.md (test spec skeleton, no test code). Design must specify: (1) the real implementation for platform.read_variable(name) -- reads from the current execution's already-resolved instance variables map (NOT a fresh Repo query per call if the instance's variables are already available in the execution context passed into the Lua sandbox; if a fresh read IS needed, specify exactly how the instance_id and prefix reach this function without ever coming from the Lua script's own arguments), applying LuaNumberMarshalling.to_lua/1 to the returned value, returning nil for an unset variable; (2) the real implementation for platform.get_instance_state(instance_id) -- MUST use a caller-supplied prefix (never derived from script input), MUST return a structured error (not a raise propagating to the Lua caller as an unhandled exception) for an invalid/nonexistent instance id; (3) the real implementation for platform.log(level, message, context) -- emits a structured log entry (Logger.log/3 or similar) tagged with the script's identity, the instance ID, and the trace ID, sourced from the execution context, never from script-supplied identity claims; (4) LuaNumberMarshalling's to_lua/1 and from_lua/1 exactly as REQ-150 Section 3 specifies (identity functions for numeric/nil cases); (5) exactly how each of the 3 functions' capability check is wired into the existing REQ-157 install/2 fold (confirm the required_capability_fun for each of these 3 matrix rows already exists correctly from REQ-157 and doesn't need to change -- only the stub_fun changes); (6) exactly what execution-context value (instance id, trace id, prefix, script identity) is threaded from the caller into Platform.install/2 (or a new parameter) so these 3 functions have what they need without ever trusting script-supplied values for tenant-boundary-relevant data. No implementation code (.ex function bodies) -- signatures, @specs, and type shapes only, describing control flow in prose/tables, never as a literal Elixir expression, however small (this exact rule has cost 3 of the 4 prior Lua-hardening designs this session at least one rework round -- grep your own draft before submitting).

Design specifies how the execution context (instance id, trace id, prefix, script identity) reaches these functions without ever trusting script-supplied values for tenant-boundary-relevant data -- explicit mechanism, not hand-waved

Design creates lib/letflow/engine/lua_number_marshalling.ex per REQ-150 Section 3's exact naming (Letflow.Engine.LuaNumberMarshalling, to_lua/1, from_lua/1) and cites REQ-150's normative section by number rather than inventing a second conversion rule
Design specifies get_instance_state returns a structured error (not an unhandled raise) for an invalid/nonexistent instance id
Design specifies log emits a structured entry carrying script identity, instance ID, and trace ID

Design confirms each function's capability requirement (variable:read, instance:read, audit:log) is unchanged from REQ-157's existing matrix rows -- only the stub_fun changes, not the required_capability_fun
Design covers all 8 acceptance criteria listed in docs/requirements.yaml's REQ-159 entry (read it directly), mapped one-to-one to concrete design elements

No implementation code (.ex function bodies) -- signatures, @specs, and type shapes only; describe control flow in prose/tables, never as a literal Elixir expression, however small -- grep your own draft for fn /raise /case /cond /do:/-> before submitting
Open questions listed explicitly if any exist, not silently resolved

REWORK ITERATION 1: CODE-DESIGN-VALIDATOR (step-01b, commit c553825) returned FAIL. Everything else in the design stands (all 8 ACs mapped, cross-tenant prefix isolation confirmed airtight, read_variable confirmed to never call Repo, log confirmed to source correlation fields only from execution_context, LuaNumberMarshalling confirmed to match REQ-150 Section 3 exactly, capability matrix confirmed unchanged) -- the ONLY defect is section 5.1's unsupported claim that get_instance_state may legitimately read ANY instance the calling tenant owns, justified by an invented 'parent instance reading a known child's state' scenario with no grounding in REQ-159's text, its 8 ACs, LUA-11/LUA-13, decision 0014, or REQ-157's capability matrix -- no parent/child instance concept exists anywhere in the read artifacts. This silently resolved a real same-tenant, cross-instance authorization question: under instance:read, any script could otherwise read every other instance's full state within the tenant. FIX (ORCH's decision, least privilege, nothing in REQ-159's text or ACs asked for broader access): restrict get_instance_state's scope by default -- the script-supplied instance_id argument must equal execution_context.instance_id; any other value returns a structured error (e.g. reason: :forbidden), not a Repo lookup against a different instance. Remove section 5.1's unsupported 'parent instance reading a known child's state' justification entirely and replace it with this restriction, stated plainly as the default scope decision (not an open question -- ORCH has decided it). Re-verify AC3 (valid/invalid instance test) still holds under this restriction: a script's own instance_id is always valid (assuming it exists), any other instance_id -- valid or not on its own terms -- is uniformly :forbidden. Re-check the rest of the document for any other place a similar unstated authorization assumption might be hiding before resubmitting. On finishing, flip this handoff's status to COMPLETED/FAILED as normal with a real result.

result.summary: REWORK ITERATION 1 fix, addressing step-01b's sole FAIL finding. Section 5.1 (get_instance_state) previously asserted, via an invented 'parent instance reading a known child's state' scenario with no grounding in REQ-159's text, its 8 ACs, LUA-11/LUA-13, decision 0014, or REQ-157's matrix, that a script may read ANY instance the calling tenant owns. Removed that justification entirely. Section 5.1 now states, as a decided default-scope policy (ORCH's call, least privilege -- nothing in REQ-159 asked for broader access): the script-supplied instance_id argument must equal execution_context.instance_id; any other value -- whether or not it names a real instance in this tenant's schema -- returns a structured {reason: "forbidden"} error with NO Repo lookup attempted, uniformly, so a script cannot use the response to probe which other instance ids exist. Section 5.2's control flow was renumbered to 5 steps: (1) no_execution_context if prefix is nil, (2) invalid_id if the argument isn't a castable UUID, (3) NEW -- forbidden if the (valid) argument != execution_context.instance_id, checked strictly before any Repo call, (4) not_found if the Repo.get for the matching self-id misses, (5) success. Section 5.3's error-reason enum gained "forbidden" as a 4th distinct value, documented as indistinguishable between a real sibling instance and a fabricated id. Section 2.1's forward reference and the section 8 traceability row for AC3 were updated to state the design's scope explicitly (self only) and note that ANY other instance_id, real or not, is uniformly forbidden -- re-verified this does not conflict with docs/requirements.yaml's actual AC3 text (read directly: 'returns instance state for a valid instance and a structured error (not a raise into the caller) for an invalid one' -- silent on cross-instance scope, so the restriction does not violate it). test/specs/REQ-159.md's test 5 (valid instance) now requires execution_context.instance_id to equal the fixture row's id; test 6 (structured errors) gained two forbidden sub-cases (a real same-tenant sibling instance, and a well-formed id that names no row at all -- both asserting the identical forbidden outcome) and clarified the not_found case as reachable only when the self-id itself has gone missing under the context's prefix, removing the now-inapplicable 'different tenant schema' not_found scenario (that case is now forbidden, not not_found, since the id check happens before any prefix-scoped query). Re-checked the rest of the document (sections 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11) for any other unstated authorization assumption: read_variable and log both source their only instance-identifying data from the closed-over execution_context, never from a script-supplied id, so no equivalent scope question exists for them; found nothing else to fix. Re-grepped both files for `fn `, `raise `, `case `, `cond `, `do:`, `->` after editing -- all remaining matches are prose false positives (e.g. 'raise shape', 'case' as an ordinary noun, 'in scope', markdown table content); no literal Elixir code introduced.
